items.title: Vijf tips voor een (nog) betere samenwerking tussen bestuurder en CISO
items.raw_text: Bestuurder en CISO gaan samen invulling geven aan de Cyberbeveiligingswet (Cbw). Het slim gestalte geven aan deze samenwerking was een van de thema’s tijdens het symposium ‘ Cbw & ggz: van regel naar regie voor bestuur en (C)iso ’. ‘Uit een kleine peiling blijkt dat zij hun samenwerking een 7,5 geven, er is dus ruimte voor verbetering.’ Uit onderzoek van de IGJ kwam onlangs naar voren dat een meerderheid van de grotere organisaties in de geestelijke gezondheidszorg (ggz) niet voldoet aan de wettelijke vereisten voor informatiebeveiliging in de zorg. De Cbw moet eraan gaan bijdragen dat (ook deze) organisaties hun cybersecurity beter op orde krijgen. De verwachting is dat de wet na de zomer van 2026 van kracht wordt. items.raw_text: By Carla Maria Martellote Viola, Senior Researcher, Brazilian Institute of Information in Science and Technology (Ibict), Brazil As governments increasingly use Artificial Intelligence (AI) to draft, organize and deliver information, a central question is becoming unavoidable: how can the integrity of government publications be protected when generative AI is part of the information-production process? In Brazil, this issue is gaining relevance alongside the Brazilian Artificial Intelligence Plan (PBIA 2024–2028), “AI for the Good of All”, which combines technological development with social inclusion, protection of rights, information integrity and responsible AI governance [1]. Information integrity involves more than factual correctness. It depends on information being accurate, complete, reliable and sufficiently contextualized, while its origin and transformations remain traceable. In institutional environments, these attributes support transparency and public trust and help reduce the risks of error, manipulation and bias. Provenance is especially important because it allows the origin, trajectory and modifications of information to be identified and its authenticity to be assessed [2]. For government publications, where citizens may rely on official information to understand rights, policies and public services, these requirements acquire particular significance. items.raw_text: By Caline Trad , IFLA-GIOPS -Information Coordinator and Dr. Jordan Srour, Interim Dean of Libraries and Information Resources, LAU Running three academic libraries across two campuses is not easy in normal times. The Lebanese American University Libraries are at the heart of our campuses; they are the space where students go to study, to meet, to learn, to explore, to create, to print or to just relax. With so much activity anything can and does happen on an average day…now add a war. LAU’s response to the renewal of Israeli hostilities on 2 March 2026, followed standard protocols: a rapid move to online learning . While moving learning online sounds easy it belies a reality of stress and anxiety with students afraid that their grades will be impacted because their bandwidth falters. Against this backdrop, the LAU Libraries made a commitment to remain open to ensure that all learners could come to campus to access stable internet and electricity. Again, not an easy decision. Opening the libraries meant requiring staff to be present on campus – even in the face of streets that were crowded with displaced Lebanese, fuel prices that multiplied, and drones that circled – and still circle – overhead. War altered the meaning of librarianship inside the three LAU libraries. Unique in the design of the Riyad Nassar Library (RNL) in Beirut, is the fact that it doubles as an airstrike shelter. items.title: From North to South: Lebanon Rising from the Ashes
items.raw_text: By Caline Trad , IFLA-GIOPS -Information Coordinator Lebanon has always been much more than a country – from North to South it is a cradle of civilization, a mosaic of faiths and a land of resilience. Lebanon’s identity is woven with pluralism, with 18 sects recognized among Christian, Islam and Druze communities. This balance is also reflected in its political system, where at the highest level of government is a Christian president and a Sunni Muslim Prime Minister, emblematic of coexistence. This diversity, though often tested, is a source of strength and cultural richness. Throughout its long history, Lebanon has offered the world treasures of intellect and spirit: from the Phoenicians who carried trade and culture across the Mediterranean, to Gibran Khalil Gibran whose words turned Beirut into a beacon of inspiration, to Fairuz whose voice is the heartbeat of a nation. On a modest stretch of just 10,452 square km, mountains guarding over generations, posts welcoming travelers, and its people rising after every storm form the land of resilience where the Lebanese spirit never dies. From Byblos, where the first alphabet was born and took shape, to the cedar forests praised in scripture, Lebanon has stood as a sanctuary of saints and prophets, a land where churches and mosques rise side by side, and where faith and culture intertwine. items.raw_text: The first day of the Metropolitan Libraries Conference (MetLib 2026) in the Netherlands brought together library professionals from around the world to explore some of the most pressing questions facing our cities and societies. The key themes of the conference were introduced during the opening speeches and an inspiring keynote by artist Julia Janssen , focusing on the growing influence of technology on our lives. During our visit to The Hague Public Library, the director Sam Hermans , welcoming participants on behalf of the G4 cities organising the conference, emphasised that technology is already transforming the future of our cities. In this changing environment, libraries must remain places of connection, bringing people together and strengthening communities. In her thought-provoking keynote, Julia Janssen explored how algorithms increasingly shape our everyday lives, often without us even realising it. Through four examples from her artistic work, she demonstrated how digital technologies can reinforce the power of profit-driven corporations and gradually undermine our ability to think critically and question the systems around us. One of her most compelling messages was the need to demystify artificial intelligence — perhaps starting by calling it what it really is: automation . items.title: LIBRARY TRANSFORMATION IN MALAYSIA From Academic Library to Innovation Ecosystem: PTTA’s Transformation at UTHM
items.raw_text: A library does not become an innovation hub simply by installing technology or adding new programs. The deeper change happens when it connects people, shares resources, and creates a lasting role across the university. Student Mobility Program Universitas Negeri Jakarta @ Drone Showcase Beyond books and buildings Perpustakaan Tunku Tun Aminah (PTTA), the academic library of Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia (UTHM), has been widening its role since 2020. Alongside its established responsibilities for collections, information access, study, and research support, the library now brings together technology showcases, cultural heritage, digital systems, student learning, and community engagement. This development reflects a broader change taking place in academic libraries. Users still need reliable access to information, but they also need places to collaborate, experiment, present ideas, preserve shared memory, and connect with expertise across the institution. For PTTA, the challenge has been to support these activities in a technical university where specialist knowledge, equipment, funding, and authority are distributed among many units. Its response has been practical: the library contributes what it already does well, including space, curation, information organisation, visibility, and trusted relationships. items.title: Authors Discuss Being Banned, Part 2: Malinda Lo, Ellen Hopkins, and Jennifer L. Armentrout
items.raw_text: The troubling trend of book challenges and bans in libraries across the US continues. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. Behind each title is an author being professionally—and sometimes personally—targeted for the stories they have chosen to share. These works usually amplify marginalized voices such as abuse victims or those within the LGBTQ+ community. American Libraries spoke with five authors on the Top 11 Most Challenged Books of 2025 list included in the report to hear how their experiences affected them. Interviews have been edited for space and clarity. Read Part 1 for the first two interviews with Patricia McCormick and Stephen Chbosky. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . items.raw_text: From the Tow-Knight Center For Journalism (CUNY): As artificial intelligence reshapes how people find and consume news, a new report from the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY examines what it will take to ensure the public has access to reliable, relevant information. The Three-Layer Cake: Public-Interest Information in an AI-Intermediated Age draws on a year of convenings and conversations with journalists, technologists, funders, investors, and other experts. It considers how journalism must evolve as AI systems increasingly stand between information providers and the people they serve. [Clip] The report outlines three connected layers: the products that identify what people want to know, the systems that synthesize answers, and the organizations that produce the underlying reporting. It also calls for greater visibility into how those systems select information and frame answers. items.raw_text: From The Star Tribune: Two Minnesota schools have been among the national leaders in library book bans the past two years, despite a law here that first banned book bans in 2024. So, if it’s illegal, how did these books get pulled from shelves? The law lacks teeth, legal experts say, because it doesn’t lay out enforcement details or potential penalties. The law prohibits public libraries from banning books based on their messages and ideas. But it lacks enforcement, said Jane Kirtley, professor emerita of media ethics and law at the University of Minnesota. “The trouble with any kind of law dealing with restrictions on speech is that it’s not self-executing,” she said. It exists and people are supposed to follow it, but with no stated consequences or enforcement means, it can be violated without punishment, Kirtley said. [Clip] A growing number of states has enacted laws against book bans, said Sarah Lamdan, executive director of the American Library Association’s Office for Intellectual Freedom. Such laws protect readers’ rights and library workers, she said. About a dozen states have them, with several more considering their own ban ban. Some states have enforcement mechanisms or do things like limit funding when a law is broken, she said. And while some state laws may lack teeth, they still indicate that a state opposes book banning, said Lynn Oberlander, a partner with the law firm Ballard Spahr. items.title: OpenAlex Announces Launch of Trusted Journal Lists
items.raw_text: From an OpenAlex Post: Trust in science is under more pressure than it has been in a long time. Paper mills, hijacked journals, citation rings and a flood of machine-written manuscripts mean that “is this a real journal?” is now a question every reader, reviewer, funder and university has to ask. And the tools for answering it have not kept up. The traditional answer is a deny list. Something like the old Beall’s List : a roster of predatory journals, so you can filter them out of a search, an evaluation, a systematic review. We understand the appeal. Nobody wants to cite a paper mill by accident. But we’re not building a deny list, and we don’t think you want one either. Librarians have been making this case for a decade : deny lists are opaque , they go stale the moment they’re published, they’re a lawsuit magnet , and they land hardest on exactly the journals that can least absorb the hit… small, new, non-English, Global South. Beall’s List went dark in 2017 . The advice since then has been consistent: don’t filter out the bad, filter in the good. Use allow lists . [Clip] In the era of the legacy indexes, “approved” meant one thing: is it in the index? That made a kind of sense when a couple of companies ran the only lists. It makes less sense now, because different questions need different lists. We launched in September with twenty-two, and we keep adding more: there are 61 now . Research habits are shifting The results show, first of all, that independent literature searching is routine for the vast majority of the surveyed students: 88.3 per cent have searched for literature or specialist information on their own, either frequently or occasionally. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. items.title: Creating Meaningful Connections Through Memory Cafés
items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. Johnson, Allan M. Kleiman, and Susan H. McFadden. Before attending this session, I had heard of Memory Cafés but did not fully understand what they were, who they served, or how they could be integrated into library programming. By the end of the hour, I felt equipped with the knowledge and resources needed to successfully bring this type of program to my own library. The library where I work is within walking distance of two senior living apartment buildings, and our community of 16,000 is also home to several assisted living facilities. Older adults often make up the majority of attendees at our programs, so as the staff member responsible for adult programming, I attended PLA hoping to learn about meaningful services for this audience. The session began by defining the core audience for a Memory Café: people living with dementia, whether formally diagnosed or not, their caregivers, and volunteers interested in learning more. items.title: From Skeptic to Troublemaker: One Book Club Idea That Changed My Mind
items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. So when I attended Tanvi Rastogi’s session, “Speak Up: Using Middle Grade Books to Build Allyship Muscles,” I assumed it would be a low-stakes hour to slowly wake up and drink my coffee. She has created a turnkey model for anyone interested in starting a chapter. Each month features a thoughtfully selected recently published title, paired with a robust downloadable discussion guide. New chapter leaders can request a starter kit complete with stickers and bookmarks mailed directly to them. items.title: Finding Connection and Community at PLA 2026

items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. What impressed me most was how scalable the ideas felt. Calgary Public Library serves nearly 1,000 employees, while my library employs roughly 30 staff members, yet many of the concepts felt immediately applicable. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials.
